hops.afterHeading: The experiment: the mark is necessary but not sufficient
hops.title: One night blindness from two different broken genes
hops.text: Oguchi disease is a rare inherited night blindness. After light exposure, the rod cells take an extremely long time to recover, so night vision comes back very slowly. Some patients have a broken arrestin gene. In other patients, researchers found mutations in the rhodopsin kinase gene. One disease can come from two genes because the kinase and arrestin work as a team to shut rhodopsin off: one writes the mark and the other reads it. Lose either partner and the off switch fails.

hops.title: How cholera toxin jams an off switch
hops.text: Cholera shows what happens when an off switch fails. In 1959, Sambhu Nath De, working in Calcutta, showed that the bacterium causes the disease by releasing a toxin. Later work revealed how that toxin acts: it blocks the GTP hydrolysis that normally turns Gs off. Gs stays active, cyclic AMP stays high, and intestinal cells secrete chloride, with water following. Jamming this one off switch drives the watery diarrhea of cholera, which can become severe.

sources.citation: Nair & Takeda, Indian J. Med. Res. 133:127 (2011)
Cassel & Selinger, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 74:3307 (1977)

hops.afterHeading: Constant GnRH shuts the pituitary down
hops.title: Why a drug that copies GnRH can shut hormones down
hops.text: You might expect a drug that copies GnRH to keep boosting reproductive hormones. At first, it does. Researchers built long-lasting copies of GnRH hoping to help fertility, and the copies did the reverse. One of them, leuprolide, sold as Lupron, was first approved to treat prostate cancer. When a man starts treatment, his testosterone often rises at first. With continued dosing, in most patients it falls to very low levels within about four weeks. A steady signal ends up shutting the system down, which is the pattern constant GnRH showed in the monkeys.

sources.citation: LUPRON DEPOT prescribing information, US FDA (2025)

audio.title: Three stories about turning signals off
audio.transcript:
Okay, scoot in. This lesson has three stories it has not told you yet, and every one of them is about an off switch.

We start in Calcutta in the nineteen fifties, with a researcher named Sambhu Nath De and a disease that can kill within hours if it goes untreated. In nineteen fifty nine, De reported something that changed how people understood cholera. The bacterium causes the disease by releasing a toxin.

Now comes the signaling twist. In nineteen seventy seven, researchers found the key to how that toxin keeps its target switched on. Researchers showed that cholera toxin blocks the GTP hydrolysis that normally switches the cyclase off. That cyclase is adenylyl cyclase, the enzyme that makes cyclic AMP. In today's language, the G protein gets stuck on. Cyclic AMP stays high, the cells of the intestine keep pushing out chloride, and water follows. The hopeful part is how simple the treatment can be. Most people with cholera can be treated successfully with an oral rehydration solution, if they get it quickly.

Story two is about a rare kind of night blindness called Oguchi disease. People with it usually have sharp daytime vision, normal side vision and normal color vision. But after light hits their rod cells, those cells take an extremely long time to recover. Eye doctors can spot something else that sounds made up. In the light, the back of the eye looks golden. After enough time in the dark it returns to a normal color, and soon after the lights come on, it turns golden again.

Here is the part that matters for this lesson. In some patients, the broken gene is arrestin. In other patients, researchers found mutations in the rhodopsin kinase gene. Two different genes, one disease. That makes sense once you remember that they work as a team. The kinase writes the mark, arrestin reads it, and if either one is missing, the receptor's off switch fails.

Our last story is about a plan that went completely backward. Researchers built strong, long lasting copies of gonadotropin releasing hormone, hoping to help people with fertility. The copies did the opposite. Given continuously, they shut the reproductive hormones down. Awkward, right? But that surprise became useful medicine. One of those drugs is leuprolide, known as Lupron, which was first approved for prostate cancer. When a man begins treatment, his testosterone often rises at first. Then, in most patients, it falls to very low levels within about four weeks.

Rhesus monkeys had already shown the rule behind this. Damage to the hypothalamus had stopped their pituitary glands from releasing gonadotropins, the hormones that drive the ovaries and testes. GnRH given once an hour brought that release back. A constant infusion did not. Same hormone, different timing, and a very different result.

So the next time a signal fades, or refuses to fade, be a little nosy and ask two questions. What is still making the signal, and what is taking it away?
